warmup.q: Two copies of the sign-up program run on two computers, and both use one database. Each copy asks the database "is there a row for @ana?", finds none, and adds one. Nothing in the database says handles must be unique, and it runs with its usual settings. The two sign-ups arrive within a millisecond. What happens?
options: The second copy waits for the first to finish, then its add fails
Both adds go through, and two users own @ana
The second check sees the first row and turns the claim down
The database notices the clash and cancels one of the two
warmup.why: Each check sees only rows that were finished (committed) before it looked, and neither add had finished yet, so both checks pass. With no row there yet, there was nothing for the second copy to wait on. Waiting and then failing is what a unique index would give you: a list inside the database that refuses a second copy of a value. Cancelling one of the two takes PostgreSQL's strictest setting, called serializable. The third option is the trap: it assumes each check sees what the other is doing at the same moment. This lesson builds that one decider without a database.

sections.h: Two people ask for @ana at once: a rule needs one decider
sections.html:
Let's replay Friday evening slowly. The payments app runs on many app servers: computers that each run a copy of the program and answer requests from phones. Handles live in a database, a program that keeps records in tables, one row per record: here, which user owns which handle.

The two sign-ups reach two different servers within a millisecond. Each server asks the database a question in SQL, the language most databases speak: SELECT ... WHERE handle = 'ana', which means "show me any row for @ana". Each finds none. So each runs INSERT, which adds a row, and commits it, which makes it permanent. Two rows now say @ana.

Why didn't the database stop it? A database makes a second writer wait by locking the row the first one is changing. But each check looked for a row that didn't exist yet, so there was nothing to lock. PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run, has a default setting called read committed. In it, each command sees only rows that others have already committed, and neither insert had committed when the other one checked. The Transactions track's lesson Write skew and phantoms met this exact shape. Inside one database the fix is a unique index, a sorted list of every handle that refuses a second copy. Both inserts of 'ana' must visit the same entry in it, so the database makes the second wait for the first, then fail.

This track builds systems from logs, lists of records that only ever grow at the end, and from copies worked out from them, spread over many machines with no single database in the middle. So what does the rule really need? Two claims for the same handle must be decided by one decider, one after the other. If two deciders can each say yes without hearing from the other, sooner or later both will. That's why the Replication track's setups with many leaders, where each region keeps its own copy and accepts writes, can't keep handles unique. Each region says yes to its own @ana, and the clash shows up after both users were told yes. Agreeing which claim came first, for everyone, is agreeing on one order, and the Consistency and consensus track showed that this is consensus.

A theatre box office has this problem every night, and an old answer. Every request for Friday's show goes to the one clerk who holds Friday's seating chart. She handles them one at a time: the first request for seat F12 gets it, and the second is told no. In our app the clerk is a processor, a program that reads requests in order, and the seating chart is its table of taken handles. The queue at her window is the log.

The simplest version has one log and one processor that does one thing at a time. The first claim for @ana in the log wins, and every later one is rejected. It's correct, but every claim in the system waits in one queue. In this lesson's simulation, 2,000 claims through one log had a p99 wait of 5,785 steps. So 99 claims in 100 waited less than that, in steps of the simulation's scheduler, which picks the task that runs next. (Latency, percentiles and the tail explains percentiles.)

The box office grows by nights, not by seats, because Friday's seats never clash with Saturday's. Claims for @bob never clash with claims for @ana either. So split the log into partitions, separate logs that each have their own processor. A claim goes to the partition picked by a hash of its handle. A hash is a number worked out from the text, always the same for the same text; the Messaging and logs track's lesson Producers I used one to pick partitions. Every claim for @ana lands in one partition, where one processor decides them in order, while claims for @bob are decided elsewhere at the same time. With 8 partitions the p99 wait fell to 2,274 steps, and no handle was given out twice. Each claim carries a request ID, the one ID per user intent from The end-to-end argument, so the phone can wait for the answer that carries its own ID.

The partition key, the value that picks the partition, is the rule. Route claims by user ID instead, and two claims for @ana from two users land in two partitions, with two processors and two tables, and both say yes. That's two clerks, each with a copy of Friday's chart. The simulation counted 937 extra owners that way, far worse than the race it was meant to fix.

The box office picture breaks at a crash. A clerk who faints still has her decisions on the chart. A crashed processor loses its memory, and gets it back only by reading its partition again, deciding the same way in the same order. Next, we'll move money, which touches two partitions.

stepper.title: Two claims for @ana meet in one partition
stepper.intro: Click through one race between two claims, decided by a log split by the handle, then by the wrong key.

sections.h: Moving money between two partitions with one logged request
sections.html:
A claim touches one partition. A transfer touches two. A user moves 8.00 from wallet w-03 to wallet w-12. The wallets are split over 4 partitions by their IDs, so w-03 lives on partition 1 and w-12 on partition 3. Each partition's processor is the only thing allowed to change its wallets' balances, the way only Friday's clerk may write on Friday's chart. So how do the debit (taking money out) and the credit (putting it in) happen together, when no single processor may do both?

The Transactions track's lesson Atomic commit across machines answered with two-phase commit. A coordinator, one program in charge of the transaction, asks both sides "can you commit?", and only when both say yes does it tell both to commit. It works, at a price. Every side must be up for every transfer, and a coordinator that dies between the two questions leaves both sides holding locks, waiting for an answer that doesn't come. A fault in one place becomes a stall everywhere.

Kleppmann, Beresford and Svingen described another way in a 2019 paper, Online Event Processing. Make one write atomic, all or nothing, and work out the rest from it. Amounts here are in cents:

  1. The client makes a request ID, t-9, and appends one message, Requested(t-9, w-03 to w-12, 800), to the partition of the wallet the money leaves. That append is the atomic step: either the request is in the log or it isn't.
  2. Processor 1 reads it in log order. It checks that w-03 holds at least 800, takes the money out of w-03, writes Credit(t-9, w-12, 800) into partition 3, and answers Accepted. If the money isn't there, it answers Declined and writes nothing else.
  3. Processor 3 reads the credit and adds 800 to w-12, unless it has already applied a credit for t-9.

Now crash processor 1 right after step 2. It restarts from its last checkpoint, a saved copy of its balances and of how far it had read, and reads the same messages in the same order. Its balances come only from those messages, so it makes the same decision and writes the same Credit(t-9, ...) a second time. Processor 3 has already seen t-9 and drops the copy. If the client hears nothing back in time and appends Requested(t-9) again, processor 1 finds t-9 among its decisions and repeats the answer without taking the money twice.

Four things make this safe. Each partition keeps its messages in order. Every message is delivered at least once, and sometimes more. Each processor decides only from what it has read, never from a clock or a random number, so a replay makes the same choices. And one request ID travels from the client to the last write, as the ID made at the tap did in The end-to-end argument.

Compare the design most teams start with. The app writes a debit to one partition and a credit to the other, two separate writes. Each processor runs balance += delta, adding the change to the balance, and saves its place in the log now and then. Nothing ties the two writes together, so they can fail apart.

The lab runs the same 1,000 transfers between 40 wallets, which hold 4,000.00 in all, under the same faults: processors that crash and replay, clients that send twice, and an app that sometimes crashes between its two writes. The separate writes end with 10,456.00 in the system, money from nowhere. 29 times the app crashed between its two writes and left a debit with no credit. 279 changes were applied twice after crashes. And 183 debits were refused for lack of funds, with nothing to stop the credits written beside them.

That last failure needs no fault at all. With every fault switched off, the two writes still end with 9,056.00, because the credit never hears that its debit was refused. The logged request ends with exactly 4,000.00. Take its request-ID checks out, and replays alone push it to 8,474.00.

Two writes can fail apart. Write one request, and derive the rest from it.

Every design in that demo shared one more thing: a moment when the 8.00 was in neither wallet. Next, we'll see why that moment is harmless, and the extra 6,456.00 isn't.

-- debit and credit as two separate writes, applied with balance += delta
   half-written transfers 29, debits refused on their own 183, steps applied twice 279
   money in the system: 1045600 (should be 400000, off by 645600)
-- the same two writes with no faults at all
   debits refused on their own 122

Amounts are in cents. The two separate writes create money even with no faults: a debit refused for lack of funds can't stop a credit that was written on its own. With faults, half-written transfers lose money and changes applied twice move it both ways, and the total ends 6,456.00 off. The logged request decides once, where the money leaves, so a refused transfer never produces a credit. Every replay after a crash still sends some credits again, which is why both of its runs send more credits than they accept transfers. Without the request-ID check each copy is added again; with it, copies are dropped and the total is exact. The runs accept slightly different numbers of transfers, because crashes change the order in which credits and requests meet.

sections.h: Late or wrong: timeliness and integrity are two different promises
sections.html:
In every design of the transfer demo, even the correct one, the credit reaches w-12's partition some time after the debit, and anyone who looks at w-12 in between sees the old balance. So the correct design was as slow as the broken ones. What separated them was what was left at the end.

The word "consistency" usually lumps together two different promises.

Timeliness means people see data that is up to date. When it breaks, you get a stale read: the credit hasn't arrived yet, or the shop's screen of today's sales is 30 seconds behind. Wait, and it goes away. Its strongest form is linearizability, from the Consistency and consensus track: every read sees the newest write, as if there were only one copy. Weaker forms promise less, such as seeing at least your own changes.

Integrity means nothing is lost, nothing is made up, and nothing contradicts anything else: every view says what the log says. When it breaks, it stays broken. A credit applied twice stays applied twice until someone finds it and writes a correction, and waiting doesn't help.

Picture a café owner at the end of the day. If her screen of today's sales trails by a minute, nobody calls the payments company. Each night, though, the company pays every shop what it took, and sends the bank a payout file that lists the amounts. If that file says 1,208.40 and the company's ledger, its list of every money movement, says 1,200.40, the owner is paid 8.00 too much. Every later payout built on that ledger carries the same error. In almost every system that holds money or records about people, integrity matters far more than timeliness. "Eventually consistent", the promise that every copy catches up in the end, is a fair promise about timeliness. It is never an excuse for an integrity bug.

A database transaction, a group of changes that happens all together or not at all, gives you both at once (the Transactions track's lesson What a transaction promises). That's why few people bother to tell them apart. The log design pulls them apart. It gets integrity from four things: the single atomic append, decisions made only from the log, and the request ID carried end to end. The fourth is a log that never changes, so any view can be replayed from it to check and repair it. The next lesson, Trust, but verify, builds that check.

None of these makes anyone wait. Timeliness you buy only where a person needs it. In Unbundling the database, a read waited until the view had applied the reader's own write, and that lab's stale reads fell from 331 in 1,000 to none. Most reads don't need that wait, so most reads don't pay for it.

A late answer heals. A wrong one stays. Guarantee integrity everywhere, and buy timeliness where someone is waiting.

Integrity everywhere sounds strict. Next, we'll see that many rules can be broken for a while, on purpose, as long as nothing is lost.

try.title: Sort six incidents into timeliness and integrity
steps: For each incident, decide: timeliness (it fixes itself if you wait) or integrity (it stays wrong until someone repairs it)?

1. A refund shows on the shop's screen 40 seconds after the app said it was done. 2. After a restart, a program that keeps balances was handed 12 ledger entries again, and added them again. 3. A search still finds a payment link that was cancelled two seconds ago. 4. The nightly payout file's total differs from the sum of the payments it lists. 5. For a few seconds after a claim, one phone shows @ana as yours and another shows it as free. 6. A program building a view met a record it couldn't read, logged a warning and moved on.
For each integrity one, write down what would catch it.
try.expect:
Timeliness: 1, 3 and 5. Each is a view that hasn't caught up yet, and each fixes itself once the change arrives. If a person can't put up with the wait, make their read wait for their own write.

Integrity: 2, 4 and 6. The 12 entries stay doubled, the payout file stays wrong, and the skipped record stays missing from the view, however long you wait. To catch them: rebuild the view from the log and compare it with the live one, check the file's total against the ledger before it is sent, and treat a record you can't read as a reason to stop, not a warning. The next lesson, Trust, but verify, builds that rebuild-and-compare check.

aside.title: Isn't "eventually consistent" a polite way of saying "sometimes wrong"?
aside.html: It's a promise about timeliness only. It says that once writes stop, every copy ends up with the same data, and it says nothing about how long that takes. A copy that is behind is late, and it will catch up. A copy that stays wrong after everything has arrived, such as a balance with a credit counted twice, isn't eventually consistent at all. It's an integrity bug, and no amount of waiting fixes it.

sections.h: Check late and say sorry: which rules really need a decider
sections.html:
Uniqueness forced every claim for one handle through one decider. Most business rules are gentler, and businesses broke them long before computers did. An airline sells more seats than the plane has, because some passengers don't turn up, and when everyone does, it pays a few to take a later flight. A shop sells its last kettle twice and emails one customer an apology and a voucher. A bank lets an account go below zero and charges a fee.

In each case the rule is checked late. A broken rule is then repaired by a compensating action, a later step that puts things right, such as a refund or a rebooking. The Transactions track's lesson Atomic commit across machines met these as the steps of a saga, a long task whose steps each have an undo.

Pat Helland and Dave Campbell put it in one line in a 2009 paper, Building on Quicksand: computing is memories, guesses and apologies. A computer acts on what it knows locally, so each action is a guess. When a guess turns out wrong, the business apologizes. Their example: "don't overbook the plane by more than 15%". Whether to coordinate, making the deciders talk before anyone says yes, becomes a business question. What does an apology cost, and what does the waiting cost? Where apologies are cheap, say yes first and check afterwards. Check first before anything you can't take back, such as sending money to a bank. Integrity still holds everywhere: an overbooked seat is a known, recorded state with a process for it, and a lost booking is not.

Peter Bailis and colleagues made "when must you coordinate?" precise, in a 2014 paper, Coordination Avoidance in Database Systems. Picture two copies of the data in two regions, starting in the same valid state. Each accepts different changes on its own, and later their changes are merged. An invariant is a rule that must always hold. It is invariant confluent if every such merge still obeys it, and a rule like that needs no coordination at all. Their table settles the common cases:

Rule, and the change Needs one decider?
a field must be filled in, or pass a check (an amount above zero), on any write no
a payment must point to a shop that exists, when a payment is added no
the same rule, when a shop is deleted yes
a name the user picks is unique (@ana) yes
an ID the system picks is unique (each region has its own range) no
IDs come in sequence with no gaps (1, 2, 3) yes
a counter with a floor, going up no
the same counter going down (a balance that must stay above zero) yes

Their prototype coordinated only where the table said it must, and ran TPC-C New-Order, a standard test that imitates a wholesale supplier taking orders, at 12.7 million transactions a second on 200 servers, 25 times the best result published before.

A year later the same group looked at what real apps do, in a paper called Feral Concurrency Control. They studied 67 open-source apps built with Rails, a popular toolkit for web apps that checks rules in the app's own code, as validations. Each model, the code for one table, declared on average 1.80 validations, against 0.13 transactions and 0.01 locks. Rails' uniqueness validation is check-then-insert, run at the database's default settings. The authors sent 64 requests at once with the same value, for 100 rounds. With no validation, all 6,300 duplicates went in. With it, 70 still got through when two running copies of the app raced, and more with more processes, up to a little under 700. With a unique index in the database, none did.

Uniqueness is not invariant confluent, and checking it in the app's code doesn't change that. Put the decision in one place: a unique index, or one partition of a log.

Every idea in this lesson trusts the machines to do what the code says: the sums come out right, and the log keeps what was written. The next lesson stops trusting them.

try.title: Which payment rules need a decider?
steps: Picture the payments app running in two regions that accept changes on their own. For each rule, decide whether each region could check it alone and still be right after their changes merge.

(a) A payment's amount is above zero. (b) Every payment points to a shop that exists, checked when the payment is added. (c) A shop can be deleted only if no payment points to it. (d) A request ID, chosen by the customer's app, is unique per shop. (e) Payout IDs are unique, made by the server. (f) A wallet's balance never goes below zero. (g) A shop's payouts add up to at most 10,000.00 a day.
For each rule that needs a decider, name the cheapest thing that would do: one partition, a unique index, or an apology.
try.expect:
No decider needed: (a) is a check on one row. (b) is the adding side of the "points to a shop" rule, and merging two sets of valid payments can't make a shop disappear. (e) works if each region makes IDs from its own range or with its own prefix.

A decider needed: (c) is the deleting side of the same rule: one region deletes the shop while the other adds a payment for it. (d) is a unique value the user's side picks: send every request for one (shop, request ID) pair to one partition, or put a unique index on it in one database. (f) and (g) are counters with a limit, pushed down by withdrawals and payouts: two regions each spend the last 50.00. Either send all of one wallet's or shop's withdrawals to one partition, which the transfer design already does, or split the budget (5,000.00 per region per day) and let a region that runs out ask the other. A business may also choose to allow a small overdraft and apologize with a fee, which is (f) checked late on purpose.

refs.title: Bailis et al., Coordination Avoidance in Database Systems (PVLDB, 2014)
Bailis et al., Feral Concurrency Control (SIGMOD, 2015)
Helland and Campbell, Building on Quicksand (CIDR, 2009)

opening:
Picture a Friday evening. The payments app, which records card payments for cafés and shops, has added wallets, so friends can send each other money by a short name called a handle. Two people named Ana sign up in the same millisecond. Both ask for @ana, and both are told it's theirs. On Saturday a friend sends 20.00 to @ana for concert tickets, and it lands with the wrong Ana.

The sign-up code looks right. It checks whether @ana is taken and, if not, saves it. It reads exactly like the rule, and it passes every test that sends one sign-up at a time.

In The end-to-end argument, one ID per tap kept a person's retries from moving money twice. Two different people who want the same thing at once need something more. In this lesson, we'll build the one decider such a rule needs from a log, move money between two parts of a system, and sort the rules that need a decider from those that can say sorry later. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with two Anas who were both told @ana was theirs. The check-then-save code wasn't wrong line by line. It had two deciders, and the fix was one: a log partition keyed by the handle, where one processor says yes or no in order.

Next time you pick a seat for a film or a concert online, watch it turn grey for everyone else while a timer starts. That's one decider per seat, holding it while you pay. When an airline asks for volunteers to take a later flight, that's an apology planned in advance.

Next, we'll stop trusting the machines themselves, and ask how a system can catch a wrong number that no part of it reported.

compare.title: Check-then-insert, and a log that decides

a.label: Check-then-insert
a.title: on each of 64 app servers
a.html: fun claim(handle: String, userId: String): Boolean { val holders = jdbc.queryForList( "SELECT user_id FROM handles WHERE name = ?", String::class.java, handle) if (holders.isNotEmpty()) return false // another server can run the same SELECT right here, and see no row either jdbc.update("INSERT INTO handles (name, user_id) VALUES (?, ?)", handle, userId) return true }

b.label: A log keyed by the handle
b.title: on the phone's side of the log
b.html: fun claim(handle: String, userId: String): Decision { val requestId = UUID.randomUUID().toString() // kept across retries of this claim val record = ProducerRecord("handle-claims", handle, Claim(requestId, userId, handle)) producer.send(record).get() // key = handle: one partition decides // a consumer of "handle-decisions" completes one future per request id return pending.getOrPut(requestId) { CompletableFuture() }.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) }

compare.note: The first version decides in 64 places at once, and hopes that no two servers' SELECT and INSERT ever interleave. The second decides in exactly one place per handle: the processor of the partition the handle hashes to. ProducerRecord and producer.send come from the client library of Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages and lets other programs read them; the record's key, the handle, picks the partition. The price is a trip through the log and a wait for the answer, the timeliness cost, and the request ID makes sure a resent claim can't count as a second one. In a single database, a unique index with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (add the row unless one with that value exists) is the same idea, with the database as the one decider.

worked.title: Follow one transfer through a crash

steps.say: The start. Partition 1 holds w-03, partition 3 holds w-12. Processor 1 last saved a checkpoint, its balances and its place, after offset 40. (An offset is a record's position in its partition.)
steps.code:
partition 1: ... [40]                 w-03 = 5,000   checkpoint after 40
partition 3: ... [17]                 w-12 = 1,000
total of the two wallets: 6,000

steps.say: The client makes request ID t-9 and appends one message. It is now stored safely, and it is the only write the client makes.
Processor 1 reads offset 41. 5,000 covers 800, so it takes the money out of w-03, writes the credit to partition 3 and answers. Then it crashes, before its next checkpoint.
steps.code:
w-03 = 4,200 (in memory)
partition 3: [18] Credit(t-9, w-12, 800)
reply: Accepted(t-9)
*** crash ***

steps.say: It restarts from the checkpoint after offset 40, so in memory w-03 holds 5,000 again. It reads offset 41 again: the same balance and the same message, so the same decision.
steps.code:
w-03 = 4,200
partition 3: [19] Credit(t-9, w-12, 800)      <- a second copy
reply: Accepted(t-9)                          <- the client already has it

steps.say: Processor 3 applies the credit at offset 18 and drops the one at 19, because t-9 is already in its set of applied credits. The two wallets hold 6,000 before and after.
steps.code:
offset 18: t-9 not seen -> w-12 = 1,800, remember t-9
offset 19: t-9 seen     -> drop
total: 4,200 + 1,800 = 6,000

lab.title: Unique handles and transfers between partitions, with no coordinator
steps: From the labs folder, run the tests once. 19 tests run and 18 fail with NotImplementedError, Kotlin's way of saying "not written yet". The one that passes is the race: checkThenInsert is finished, and it gives handles out twice. Scheduler.kt is finished too. It runs the tasks in a random order picked from a fixed seed, so every count comes out the same on every run.
In Claims.kt, write partitionFor. Then write ClaimProcessor.decide. You need two maps: one from handle to owner, and one from request ID to the decision already given. Run ClaimsTest.
Read throughLog (finished) and find the one line that picks a partition. The test keyed by userId instead... passes a different key to your own code. Watch it give handles out twice.

In Transfers.kt, write WalletProcessor.handle. The comment above it lists three cases for a request and one for a credit. Run TransfersTest. assertIntegrity, at the bottom of the file, lists exactly what must still hold after crashes, replays and resent requests. Two tests run the broken design, runSeparateSteps (finished), under the same faults: read it and find the two writes that nothing ties together.
When everything passes, delete the duplicate check for credits and run TransfersTest again. Which tests fail, and which line of assertIntegrity catches it first?
hints: partitionFor: Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), partitions). floorMod keeps the result between 0 and partitions - 1, even when the hash is negative.

decide: if decided[claim.requestId] is there, return it. Otherwise grant the claim when the holder is null or is the same user, and reject it otherwise. Store the decision under the request ID before you return it.
handle for a Requested: look in outcomes first, and reply with what you find there. Debit and call send only when balances.getValue(t.from) covers the amount, and record the outcome either way.
handle for a Credit: creditsApplied.add(msg.requestId) returns false when the ID was already there. Return early in that case.

drill.title: Rules through a log, from memory
drill.prompt: Without notes: (1) write partitionFor and the rule for deciding one claim, in about six lines; (2) list the four things that make a transfer between two partitions safe; (3) say what timeliness and integrity mean, in one sentence each, with one example of each one breaking; (4) name two rules that are not invariant confluent.

answer.html:
(1) partitionFor(key, n) = Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), n)
    decide(c): if c.requestId was answered, return that answer
               holder = owner[c.username]
               if holder == null or holder == c.userId: owner[c.username] = c.userId; Granted
               else Rejected(held by holder); remember the answer under c.requestId
(2) order within each partition; at-least-once delivery;
    processors whose decisions depend only on what they read;
    one request id from the client to the last write, checked at every consumer
(3) timeliness: users see up-to-date state; violation: a stale read that fixes
    itself (the credit shows up 200 ms later)
    integrity: nothing lost, invented or contradictory; violation: permanent
    (a credit applied twice stays applied twice)
(4) uniqueness of a value the user chooses; a counter with a lower bound under
    decrements (balance >= 0); also foreign-key deletes and sequential IDs

recap: A rule like "every handle has one owner" needs one decider per value. Send every claim for a value to one log partition, picked by that value, and let one processor decide the claims in order.
The partition key is the rule. Route claims by anything else, such as the user ID, and two processors each say yes, with no error anywhere.

A transfer between two partitions needs no two-phase commit. One appended request is the all-or-nothing step, and the debit and the credit are worked out from it by processors that decide only from what they read and drop repeats by request ID.
Timeliness problems (stale reads) heal if you wait; integrity problems (lost, doubled or contradictory data) stay. Guarantee integrity everywhere, and buy timeliness where someone is waiting.

Many rules can be checked late and put right with an apology. Invariant confluence says which can't: a unique name the user picks, and a balance that must stay above zero, need one decider; most other rules don't.
The limit: one partition orders only its own records, and the one decider for a busy value is a queue that everyone waits in. And all of it assumes the machines compute and store what the code says.

explain.prompt: A friend says: "A log can't enforce a rule like unique handles. For that you need a lock across all the servers, or a database." Explain how a log split into partitions keeps handles unique, what it costs, and the one mistake that breaks it.
explain.answer: The rule needs one decider for each handle, not a database. If every claim is sent to a partition picked by its handle, all the claims for one handle land in the same partition, and one processor reads that partition in order, one claim at a time. It keeps a table of taken handles, grants the first claim for each handle and rejects the rest, and remembers each request ID, so a claim delivered twice gets the same answer twice. Its table comes only from the partition, so after a crash it reads the partition again and decides the same way. Claims for different handles go to different partitions and are decided at the same time, so it grows by adding partitions. The cost is timeliness: the phone must append its claim and then wait for the answer, which is a trip through the log. The mistake that breaks it is picking the partition by anything other than the handle, such as the user ID. Then two claims for one handle reach two processors with separate tables, and both are granted, with no error anywhere.

deeper.html:
Splitting a budget. A daily payout limit of 10,000.00 per shop is a counter with a ceiling, so two regions can't each check it alone. They can if you split it: give each region 5,000.00 to spend without asking, and let a region that runs low ask the other for part of its share. Building on Quicksand discusses escrow, a related scheme for changes that can be applied in any order, such as adding and subtracting. Work on CRDTs, data types built so that copies can merge without coordination (the Replication track's lesson Concurrent writes), calls the replicated form a bounded counter. The trade is plain: no coordination on the common path, a little on the rare one.

Reading is not deciding. A sign-up form that shows "@ana is available" as you type is reading a view, and the view may be stale. That's fine, as long as the claim itself goes through the processor and the user is told the real answer. Treat every check made outside the decider as a hint for the screen, never as the decision.

Where the order runs out. One partition orders the claims for one handle. Nothing orders a claim on partition 0 against a transfer on partition 3. Rules that relate records in different partitions ("a user may hold at most three handles") need those records sent to one partition together, or a second step that checks and repairs. Data integration, the first lesson of this track, showed where a single order for everything stops; past that point, an order per key is all you get.

The handle-claim and transfer designs are discussed in Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, a well-known book on these systems, in chapter 13, which builds on the Online Event Processing paper cited above.
